entries.title: Positive part in the nontransitive boundary bound
entries.locator: arXiv:2106.06400v3, Lemma 2.1 and its proof, printed pages 11–12.
entries.claim: The boundary susceptibility is bounded below using the square of the minimum-susceptibility deficit, without taking its positive part.
entries.problem: The deficit can be negative. An inequality bounding it above by a nonnegative Cauchy–Schwarz expression cannot be squared in that case. JTBG gives a connected three-vertex counterexample with finite susceptibilities and weight rows at most one.
entries.correction: 67GX replaces the squared deficit by its squared positive part, and first proves the stronger bound using the actual nonnegative mass leaving the set. Under constant susceptibility the positive part can be omitted. This correction does not change the transitive use of that boundary lemma.
entries.leanImpact: The nontransitive target is 67GX with the positive-part square (or the stronger outgoing-mass bound). JTBG records why the unsigned square cannot be the general target. A source wrapper may remove the positive part only after establishing constant susceptibility; the transitive application is unchanged. Merged private lrp at 22d8485da86b12aa41d1985b07939d2e6e612e26 now contains the corrected boundary and deletion arguments in PercLib/Percolation/Bond/BoundarySusceptibility.lean and the explicit counterexample in PercLib/Models/BoundaryCounterexample.lean. The 31-contract source inventory records their hypotheses, zero-denominator conventions and witnesses. This is source-inspected progress only; matching compiled tag associations and fingerprint-bound correspondence reviews remain separate, and the published-paper entry stays provisional.

resolution.summary: Square only the positive part of the boundary deficit.
resolution.impact: The general boundary inequality must be weakened; its constant-susceptibility transitive use is unchanged.

entries.title: The stronger quantitative triangle numerator
entries.locator: arXiv:2106.06400v3, equations (2.4)–(2.5) and their Cauchy–Schwarz derivation, printed page 12.
entries.claim: The source gives a susceptibility lower derivative bound with numerator chi times (chi minus the triangle diagram), over the stated quadratic diagram denominator.
entries.problem: The displayed Cauchy–Schwarz inputs yield a squared positive-part deficit instead. MTYL gives a normalized infinite-line counterexample to the stronger formula at small positive intensity; 1EWX shows the same small-intensity obstruction for normalized transitive models with finite critical point.
entries.correction: 4KBG proves chi-prime at least (chi minus Delta)_+ squared divided by 3 beta squared Delta squared, almost everywhere, under its stated transitivity, mass-transport, row-sum and finite-susceptibility hypotheses. It retains the bounded-triangle susceptibility consequence but is weaker than the source formula. OVWJ recovers the hierarchical off-critical upper bounds under explicit endpoint two-point and boundary-flux assumptions; WPAD gives the resulting tail and density bounds. On the chosen finite-ball interval, the triangle is eventually at most half the susceptibility, so the corrected square suffices.
entries.leanImpact: The replacement target is the weaker differential inequality 4KBG, including its almost-everywhere qualification. MTYL and 1EWX distinguish the false stronger numerator from this target. A formal proof of the replacement cannot certify the stronger source formula; the bounded-triangle consequence needs the separate integration argument. The hierarchical application additionally needs 6F2J, the finite-ball form of 4KBG with the row-normalization factor, the triangle estimate MS6M, threshold convergence and the logarithmic inversion in OVWJ. WPAD uses X8T6. This does not discharge the endpoint assumptions or provide a Lean proof; source confirmation is still pending. Source-inspected update at merged private lrp 3978a2fa0ec425729f6e15fbc3c6a142cfa4a672: PercLib/Models/NormalizedSmallIntensityLine.lean now proves the exact MTYL line formulas and the strict obstruction throughout 0 < beta < 1/48. PercLib/Models/NormalizedSmallIntensity.lean proves the numerical bounds in 1EWX without needing transitivity, but does not prove its derivative assertion. The 44-contract normalization inventory records both files. These implementations formalize the obstruction, not the replacement inequality or its hierarchical application; compiled tag association and correspondence review are not inferred, and this erratum remains provisional.

resolution.summary: Use the proved squared positive-part deficit in the susceptibility differential inequality.
resolution.impact: The printed stronger formula is false. Bounded-triangle consequences survive; hierarchical consequences need the stated additional inputs.

entries.title: The transcript entropy estimate retains the squared intensity difference
entries.locator: arXiv:2106.06400v3, proof of Theorem 3.1, equation (3.6) and the first factor in (3.7), printed page 19. Checked in PDF text and HTML; the typeset journal version has not been checked.
entries.claim: The finite-transcript bound (3.6) and the first expression on the right of (3.7) use $|\beta_1-\beta_2|$, although the preceding single-query bound and the final expression in (3.7) use $|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2$.
entries.problem: The linear factor is false in general. Let a tree reveal the single edge of a two-vertex graph, with weight $J=1/10$ and intensities $\beta_1=10$, $\beta_2=20$. Set $t=e^{-1}$. Its transcript entropy is $D=t-(1-t)\log(1+t)\geq t^2=e^{-2}>1/20$, using $\log(1+t)\leq t$ and $e<3$. The printed right-hand side is $|10-20|J/(2\min\{10,20\})=1/20$. Thus the discrepancy is not just an alternative weaker bound.
entries.correction: Restore $|\beta_1-\beta_2|^2$ in (3.6) and in the first factor of (3.7). KHB7 bounds each queried Bernoulli coordinate by $J_e(\beta_1-\beta_2)^2/(2\min\{\beta_1,\beta_2\})$. CH4N sums these costs with revealments under the first law. For positive intensities and finite weighted cost, D66F then passes from finite transcripts to a common Borel output by finite-prefix approximation. This repairs the proof without changing the final entropy comparison or its cluster-tail consequence; infinite cost and zero intensities are not treated by division.
entries.leanImpact: The coordinate entropy bound, transcript chain rule and weighted revealment sum must retain the squared parameter difference. The existing tagged prose already has that square and needs no statement change. A formal source wrapper should target the final comparison with its positive-intensity and finite-cost qualifications, not the false intermediate linear-factor inequality. These prose links do not certify a compiled entropy proof.

resolution.summary: Restore the squared intensity difference in the entropy estimates.
resolution.impact: Repairs the coordinate and transcript calculations; the final entropy and cluster-tail comparison are unchanged.

entries.title: The hierarchical Fourier transform uses a compact product dual
entries.locator: arXiv:2106.06400v3, last paragraph of Section 2 after equation (2.10), printed page 15. Checked in PDF text and HTML; the typeset journal version has not been checked.
entries.claim: The paragraph treats the Fourier transform of a summable function on the discrete hierarchical lattice as a function on that same lattice, and identifies the lattice with its Pontryagin dual.
entries.problem: For $A=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, $d\geq1$, $L\geq2$, the discrete group $H=\bigoplus_{i\geq1}A$ has dual $K=\prod_{i\geq1}\widehat A\cong\prod_{i\geq1}A$, not the direct sum. Every sequence of coordinate characters defines a character of $H$, since an element of $H$ has finite support; conversely its restrictions to the coordinate groups determine it. The dual topology is the product topology. Thus $H$ is countable and discrete while $K$ is uncountable and compact. Restriction to finite-support characters does not supply a dual counting measure: the transform of the point mass at zero is the constant one, which is not square-summable for counting measure on $H$.
entries.correction: For $f\in\ell^1(H)$, use $\widehat f(y)=\sum_{x\in H}f(x)\exp(2\pi i\sum_{j\geq1}x_j\cdot y_j/L)$ for $y\in K$. The inner sum is finite. Use counting measure on $H$ and normalized product Haar measure on $K$ in inversion, convolution and the integrals. This supplies the correct dual setting for the summable-kernel Fourier argument. Alternatively, the existing 87W3 and IZAO proofs compare the diagrams through finite positive matrices and an invariant trace, avoiding this Fourier identification entirely. Their finite-susceptibility conclusions are unchanged.
entries.leanImpact: Do not introduce a self-duality equivalence for the discrete hierarchical direct sum. A Fourier formalisation needs the compact product of character groups and its normalized Haar measure. The matrix-and-trace route CS16 to 87W3 or IZAO is an alternative dependency chain for the needed diagram bound, under its own summability and invariance hypotheses; it does not certify the incorrect dual-group identification. No compiled Fourier correspondence is asserted.

resolution.summary: Use the compact product dual with normalized Haar measure, or the finite-matrix proof.
resolution.impact: The Fourier framework needs replacement; the finite-susceptibility diagram comparisons survive.

entries.title: Finite restrictions do not supply a uniform positive lower bound
entries.locator: Appendix A, proof of Theorem A.5, printed pp. 30–31. Checked in arXiv v3 PDF text and HTML; the typeset journal edition has not been checked.
entries.claim: The proof says that an infinite matrix is positive definite if and only if every finite principal submatrix is, after defining positive definite to require one strictly positive uniform lower bound.
entries.problem: The diagonal matrix D(n,n)=1/n on the positive integers has strictly positive finite principal matrices but no uniform lower bound. The tensor-product comment likewise needs positive semidefinite, rather than positive definite, for possibly singular factors.
entries.correction: Use positive semidefinite throughout the finite-restriction argument. Alternatively require one fixed lower bound for every restriction. The Schur theorem as stated is unchanged; TAB8 proves it with finite Gram matrices and proves the bounded operator norm estimate separately.
entries.leanImpact: The finite-principal-matrix equivalence concerns nonnegative quadratic forms. A bounded inverse needs a single positive coercivity constant, not separate constants for each finite set. No new compiled matrix or inverse theorem is asserted.

resolution.summary: Use positive semidefiniteness, or require a uniform positive lower bound.
resolution.impact: Repairs the finite-restriction argument; the Schur theorem itself is unchanged.

entries.title: The semidefinite Ando proof cannot assume inverses
entries.locator: Appendix A, proof of Theorem A.6, printed p. 33. Checked in arXiv v3 PDF text and HTML; the typeset journal edition has not been checked.
entries.claim: The theorem allows commuting positive semidefinite bounded operators, but its proof writes their inverses and applies Lemma A.7, which requires a uniform positive lower bound.
entries.problem: A positive semidefinite operator can be singular, including the zero operator. Even injective positive bounded operators need not have bounded inverses. Commutativity supplies neither condition.
entries.correction: Factor the two block quadratic forms as squared norms using S^(1/2) and T^(1/2). Their commutativity identifies the cross term with (ST)^(1/2). Schur positivity and evaluation at (f,-f) then prove the claimed inequality directly, including singular operators. The percolation application also has a separate singleton lower bound, but that does not repair the stated general theorem by itself.
entries.leanImpact: Keep the general target positive semidefinite. Use the Gram block factorization, or explicitly add and then remove a positive regularization. Do not infer an inverse from nonnegative quadratic forms. The inequality and its diagram application are unchanged; compiled correspondence remains outstanding.

resolution.summary: Factor the block forms with square roots instead of taking inverses.
resolution.impact: A short proof replacement covers singular positive operators and retains the theorem.

entries.title: The square-root norm uses exponent one half
entries.locator: Appendix A, proof of Lemma A.9, first norm estimate, printed p. 34. Checked in arXiv v3 PDF text and HTML; the typeset journal edition has not been checked.
entries.claim: The norm of a conjugated positive square root is bounded by the square of the original operator norm.
entries.problem: For T=I/4 and a unit vector, the square-root norm is 1/2 while the displayed bound gives 1/16. The assertion of the lemma remains true.
entries.correction: Use ||T^(1/2)||=||T||^(1/2). Unitary conjugation preserves positivity and squares, so uniqueness of the positive square root proves invariance directly.
entries.leanImpact: A norm lemma must retain exponent one half. The invariant-root target needs bounded positivity and the permutation action, without transitivity or mass transport. No change to the trace or diagram conclusion and no compiled root theorem are inferred.

resolution.summary: Use the square-root operator norm exponent one half.
resolution.impact: Corrects the display; uniqueness of the positive square root gives the same invariance result.
